articles.title: Accuracy of Autonomous Artificial Intelligence-Based Diabetic Retinopathy Screening in Real-Life Clinical Practice
articles.snippet: Background: In diabetic retinopathy, early detection and intervention are crucial in preventing vision loss and improving patient outcomes. In the era of artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning, new promising diagnostic tools have emerged. The IDX-DR machine (Digital Diagnostics, Coralvill
articles.full_summary: This study compared the IDX-DR AI system to human graders for diabetic retinopathy screening, finding 100% sensitivity for 'no DR', 'mild DR', and 'moderate DR', but also that the AI system tended to overestimate DR stages.
articles.key_finding: Sensitivity was calculated to be 100% for 'no DR', 'mild DR', and 'moderate DR'.
articles.population: patients undergoing AI-based DR screening

articles.title: Comparison of Validity and Reliability of Manual Consensus Grading vs. Automated AI Grading for Diabetic Retinopathy Screening in Oslo, Norway: A Cross-Sectional Pilot Study.
articles.snippet: Karabeg M, Petrovski G, Holen K, Steffensen Sauesund E, Fosmark DS, Russell G et al. | Journal of clinical medicine | 2025-Jul-07 | Journal Article
articles.full_summary: This cross-sectional pilot study compared the validity and reliability of automated AI-based grading (EyeArt) with manual consensus grading for diabetic retinopathy screening, reporting high sensitivity for the AI system.
articles.key_finding: Prevalence of any vs. referable DR (RDR) was 20.2% vs. 11.7%, while sensitivity was 94.0% vs. 89.7%, specificity was 72.6% was 83.0%, and AUC was 83.5% vs. 86.3%, respectively.
articles.population: patients (≥18 years) with diabetes

articles.title: Autonomous artificial intelligence versus teleophthalmology for diabetic retinopathy.

articles.title: Comparative assessment of diagnostic agreement between artificial intelligence and general practitioners in diabetic retinopathy screening using non-mydriatic fundus photography.
articles.snippet:
AIMS
To assess the diagnostic agreement between an artificial intelligence (AI) system and general practitioners (GPs) interpreting fundus photographs for diabetic retinopathy (DR) screening, using the ophthalmologists' assessment as the reference standard.


METHODS
We performed a cross-sectional s
articles.full_summary: This study compares an AI system to general practitioners for diabetic retinopathy screening, finding the AI system had higher sensitivity and diagnostic agreement than GPs when compared to an ophthalmologist reference standard.
articles.key_finding: AI showed near-perfect agreement with ophthalmology (κ = 0.91) and outperformed GPs, with 98.2% sensitivity, 98.9% specificity, and 98.8% accuracy.

articles.title: Use in clinical practice of an automated screening method of diabetic retinopathy that can be derived using a diagnostic artificial intelligence system.
articles.snippet: Peris-Martínez C, Shaha A, Clarida W, Amelon R, Hernáez-Ortega MC, Navea A et al. | Archivos de la Sociedad Espanola de Oftalmologia | 2021-Mar | Journal Article
articles.full_summary: An autonomous AI system showed 100% sensitivity for detecting referable diabetic retinopathy (RDR) and vision-threatening diabetic retinopathy (VTDR) when compared to manual classification by ophthalmologists.
articles.key_finding: The AI system recorded 100% (95% CI: 97-100%) sensitivity and 81.82% (95% CI: 80 -83%) specificity for RDR, and 100% (95% CI: 95-100%) of sensitivity and 94.64% (95% CI: 94-95%) of specificity for VTDR.

articles.title: Comparison of automated and expert human grading of diabetic retinopathy using smartphone-based retinal photography.
articles.snippet: Kim TN, Aaberg MT, Li P, Davila JR, Bhaskaranand M, Bhat S et al. | Eye (London, England) | 2021-Jan | Journal Article; Research Support, N.I.H., Extramural; Research Support, Non-U.S. Gov't
articles.full_summary: This study compared automated and expert human grading of diabetic retinopathy using smartphone-based retinal photography, finding automated interpretation had lower sensitivity but higher specificity than trained expert graders.
articles.key_finding: At the patient-level, automated interpretation had a sensitivity of 87.0% and specificity of 78.6%; grader 1 had a sensitivity of 96.3% and specificity of 42.9%; grader 2 had a sensitivity of 92.5% and specificity of 50.0%.
articles.population: 119 eyes from 69 patients with diabetes

articles.title: Systematic review and meta-analysis of regulator-approved deep learning systems for fundus diabetic retinopathy detections.

articles.title: Performance of a Deep-Learning Algorithm vs Manual Grading for Detecting Diabetic Retinopathy in India.
articles.snippet:

articles.full_summary: This study validated an automated DR system against manual grading by trained graders and retina specialists in an Indian population, finding the automated system's performance was equal to or exceeded manual grading.

articles.title: Pivotal trial of an autonomous AI-based diagnostic system for detection of diabetic retinopathy in primary care offices
articles.snippet: Artificial Intelligence (AI) has long promised to increase healthcare affordability, quality and accessibility but FDA, until recently, had never authorized an autonomous AI diagnostic system. This pivotal trial of an AI system to detect diabetic retinopathy (DR) in people with diabetes enrolled 900
articles.full_summary: This pivotal trial evaluated an autonomous AI system for detecting diabetic retinopathy in primary care, demonstrating that the AI system exceeded pre-specified superiority endpoints for sensitivity and specificity.
articles.key_finding: The AI system exceeded all pre-specified superiority endpoints at sensitivity of 87.2% (95% CI, 81.8–91.2%) (>85%), specificity of 90.7% (95% CI, 88.3–92.7%) (>82.5%), and imageability rate of 96.1% (95% CI, 94.6–97.3%), demonstrating AI’s ability to bring specialty-level diagnostics to primary care settings.
articles.population: 900 subjects with no history of DR at primary care clinics

response.global_summary:
Autonomous artificial intelligence (AI) systems for diabetic retinopathy (DR) screening generally demonstrate high sensitivity, often comparable to or exceeding that of human expert graders, particularly for detecting referable or vision-threatening DR [2][3][5][7][8][9][10][11][13][14][15][16][18][19]. Several studies highlight the potential for AI to improve screening efficiency and access, especially in primary care settings [10][15].

For instance, a 2023 controlled trial comparing the EyeArt AI system with ophthalmologists' dilated examinations found that the AI system identified **36 of 37 eyes as positive** for more than mild DR (mtmDR), achieving a sensitivity of **97%**, while retina specialists identified **22 of 37 eyes as positive** (sensitivity **59.5%**) [2]. Similarly, general ophthalmologists in the same study had a sensitivity of **20.6%** [2]. A 2026 cross-sectional study in primary care patients with type 2 diabetes reported that AI showed near-perfect agreement with ophthalmology (kappa = **0.91**) and outperformed general practitioners, with **98.2% sensitivity**, **98.9% specificity**, and **98.8% accuracy** [10].

Multiple cohort studies and systematic reviews support these findings. A 2024 cohort study calculated AI sensitivity to be **100%** for 'no DR', 'mild DR', and 'moderate DR' [0]. Another cohort study from 2021 reported **100% sensitivity** for referable DR (RDR) and vision-threatening DR (VTDR) in a Spanish population, with specificities of **81.82%** and **94.64%**, respectively [19]. A 2021 study on an AI system in clinical practice also found **100% sensitivity** for RDR and VTDR [11]. A 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis found that AI had higher pooled sensitivity than store-and-forward (SAF) methods for any DR (**86.9% vs 80.9%**), RDR (**96.2% vs 88.6%**), VTDR (**96.2% vs 84.2%**), and DME (**97.2% vs 87.4%**) [3]. A 2026 meta-analysis of regulator-approved deep learning systems reported pooled sensitivity of **0.93** per-patient and **0.92** per eye, closely paralleling expert grading [13].

Specific AI systems, such as EyeArt, have been extensively evaluated. A 2026 meta-analysis of 162,695 examinations with EyeArt showed a pooled sensitivity of **95%** and specificity of **81%** [8]. A 2017 cohort study reported EyeArt sensitivity at **94.7%** for any retinopathy and **93.8%** for referable retinopathy [4]. A large prospective evaluation of EyeArt in over 30,000 patients in English screening programs found a sensitivity of **95.7%** for referable retinopathy [18]. Other AI models have also shown high performance, with one study reporting sensitivities of **95%** and **94%** for two models compared to a gold standard [6].

However, some studies present **mixed or lower sensitivity results** for AI systems. A 2025 cross-sectional pilot study in Oslo, Norway, found AI sensitivity for any DR to be **94.0%** and for referable DR to be **89.7%**, with specificities of **72.6%** and **83.0%**, respectively [1]. A 2026 cohort study in a Tanzanian population found that sensitivity for detecting referable DR across four commercially available AI systems ranged from **83.9% to 93.7%**, with lower specificity ranging from **70.3% to 79.0%** [17]. A 2021 study comparing automated and expert human grading using smartphone-based retinal photography found that automated interpretation had a sensitivity of **87.0%** and specificity of **78.6%**, while human graders achieved higher sensitivities of **96.3%** and **92.5%** [12]. In the 2017 cohort study, while EyeArt performed well, another system, Retmarker, showed lower sensitivities of **73.0%** for any retinopathy and **85.0%** for referable retinopathy [4].

key_findings.text: Autonomous AI systems for diabetic retinopathy screening generally achieve high sensitivity, often comparable to or exceeding that of human expert graders, particularly for detecting referable or vision-threatening diabetic retinopathy.

The EyeArt AI system has demonstrated high sensitivity for detecting diabetic retinopathy, with pooled sensitivity of 95% across a large number of examinations and specific instances of 97% for more than mild DR.
AI systems can achieve 100% sensitivity for detecting 'no DR', 'mild DR', 'moderate DR', referable DR, and vision-threatening DR in certain clinical settings.

AI systems show higher pooled sensitivity compared to store-and-forward methods for various stages of diabetic retinopathy, including any DR, referable DR, vision-threatening DR, and diabetic macular edema.
AI systems can outperform general practitioners in diabetic retinopathy screening, demonstrating near-perfect agreement with ophthalmology.
Some AI systems may exhibit lower specificity, ranging from 70.3% to 83.0%, even when sensitivity is high.
The performance of AI systems can vary, with some systems showing lower sensitivities (e.g., 73.0% for any retinopathy) compared to others.

disagreements.issue: The comparative sensitivity of automated AI interpretation versus human graders for diabetic retinopathy detection using smartphone-based retinal photography.
positions: Automated interpretation has lower sensitivity (87.0%) compared to human graders (96.3% and 92.5%) [12].
AI systems can achieve sensitivity similar to or exceeding that of experts [2][5][10].

evidence_gaps: The sources do not consistently report on the long-term impact of autonomous AI screening on patient outcomes, such as progression of DR or visual acuity.

There is limited information on the cost-effectiveness of various AI systems compared to human grading in diverse healthcare settings, beyond a single mention of cost-effectiveness as a comparison point [4].
The sources do not provide a detailed breakdown of AI performance across different ethnic groups or populations with varying prevalence of DR, which could influence generalizability.

The sources do not extensively discuss the implications of AI's varying specificity on patient management, such as the potential for increased false positives and subsequent burden on ophthalmology services.
